endorsements.title: Utah HB 452 (2025), mental health chatbots
endorsements.quote: (viii) implements protocols to respond in real time to acute risk of physical harm;

endorsements.title: Preparing AI chatbots to respond to patient distress and suicidality in high-risk healthcare settings
endorsements.quote: We recommend that all implementers building AI chatbots to support behavioral health services consider adopting this or a similar safety monitoring approach that executes rigorous safety guardrails beyond those already available through LLM providers like OpenAI 12.

endorsements.title: Large language models could change the future of behavioral healthcare: a proposal for responsible development and evaluation
endorsements.quote: Accurate risk detection and mandated reporting are crucial aspects that clinical LLMs must prioritize, particularly in the identification of suicidal/homicidal ideation, child/elder abuse, and intimate partner violence.

endorsements.title: From Skepticism to Support: Addressing Clinician and Patient Concerns About AI in Eating Disorder Care
endorsements.issuer: The International journal of eating disorders
endorsements.quote: Multiple technical guardrails must be implemented, such as safety classifiers for high-risk content (e.g., suicidality) and filters to prevent harmful generation.

endorsements.title: Expert Consensus Best Practices for the Safe, Ethical, and Effective Design and Implementation of Artificially Intelligent Conversational Agent (i.e., Chatbot/Virtual Human) Systems in Health Care Applications
endorsements.quote: Optimally, for users interacting with an AICA for mental health purposes, the chatbot should have defined protocols to detect patients in crisis and have the capability to direct them to easily accessible human resources or emergency medical services for immediate help.

endorsements.title: Commentary: AI psychosis is not a new threat: Lessons from media-induced delusions
endorsements.quote: In clinical products, route concerning conversations to trained staff when thresholds are met, and log safety alerts.

endorsements.title: A Prompt Engineering Framework for Large Language Model-Based Mental Health Chatbots: Conceptual Framework
endorsements.quote: When a crisis has been detected (eg, overt suicidal thinking), the system initiates an emergency response (eg, providing crisis hotline numbers or pinging a human therapist) before any engagement with an LLM.

endorsements.title: Conversational AI for perinatal mental health: promise, limits, and a human-AI stepped-care framework
endorsements.quote: For crisis-level signals such as suicidality, infant harm ideation, or indicators of postpartum psychosis, the system must bypass generative AI entirely and route deterministically to emergency protocols, consistent with the Language Detection Protocol (LDP) approach validated in perinatal chatbot deployment ( 13 ).

endorsements.title: Generative AI as a de facto mental health provider: a policy brief and urgent call for regulation
endorsements.quote: GenAI platforms must incorporate robust mechanisms to detect indicators of acute psychological crisis.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence in traumatic stress treatment: The TRUST framework for ethical development, clinical applications, and research advancement
endorsements.quote: During deployment, crisis escalation protocols with defined response times must be implemented and actively monitored, “human-in-the-loop” oversight for high-risk situations must be maintained, real-time safety monitoring interfaces should be used, and defined check-ins with clinicians engaging with the AI tool should be prioritized.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) psychosis: mechanisms, clinical risks and safety considerations in generative AI chatbots
endorsements.quote: These measures should be accompanied by robust crisis detection and escalation pathways that enable rapid connection to human support when risk signals emerge.

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: Crisis management requires a distinct escalation protocol that includes detection of self-harm, suicide, or interpersonal violence signals; immediate, nonjudgmental acknowledgment; safety-oriented risk stratification; delivery of context-appropriate crisis resources; and handoff to human crisis support where available [ 6 , 28 , 112 , 119 ].

endorsements.title: AI as a Therapist, Companion, and Romantic Partner: Emerging Roles, Benefits, and Risks for Mental Health in Participatory Medicine
endorsements.quote: AI systems should be designed to detect clinical risk, reduce friction in accessing help, and maintain a connection with the user throughout the transition.

endorsements.title: The interactive turn in generative AI for self-harm
endorsements.quote: It must handle disclosure of imminent risk with clear protocols for escalation.

endorsements.title: AI Therapy Chatbots in Youth With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Nurse-Led, Risk-Tiered Policy Framework
endorsements.quote: When a high-risk flag is triggered, the system initiates an alert to the designated nurse within a predefined time window (eg, immediate escalation for imminent risk and within 24 hours for high-risk but nonimminent flags), prompting nurse-led assessment and triage.

evidence.title: Beyond Simulations: What 20,000 Real Conversations Reveal About Mental Health AI Safety
evidence.outcome: Harmful content rates, purpose-built AI with layered safeguards vs general-purpose LLMs
evidence.effect: Harmful content lower for the purpose-built AI: suicide/NSSI .4-11.27% vs 29.0-54.4%; eating disorder 8.4% vs 54.0%; substance use 9.9% vs 45.0%.
evidence.quote: The purpose-built AI was significantly less likely than general-purpose LLMs to produce harmful content across suicide/NSSI (.4-11.27% vs 29.0-54.4%), eating disorder (8.4% vs 54.0%), and substance use (9.9% vs 45.0%) benchmarks.

evidence.title: Safety Evaluation of a Generative AI Agent for Anxiety and Depression Symptoms
evidence.outcome: Safety risk in real-user responses under multi-agent safety system with automated harm detection and clinician oversight
evidence.effect: No AI-generated responses among 12,040 real-user responses contained AI content safety risk (95% CI 0.00%, 0.04%); no serious adverse events occurred.
evidence.quote: In Study Two (observational study), no AI-generated responses were identified as containing AI content safety risk (95% CI: 0.00%, 0.04%), and no serious adverse events occurred.
evidence.sample_unit: AI-generated responses (43,325 simulated; 12,040 real-user; 111 adults in Study Two)

evidence.title: Vickybot, a Chatbot for Anxiety-Depressive Symptoms and Work-Related Burnout in Primary Care and Health Care Professionals: Development, Feasibility, and Potential Effectiveness Studies
evidence.outcome: Suicide alert detection and research team response to acute suicide risk in chatbot users
evidence.effect: Suicidal alerts were received correctly in simulation; 9% (3/34) of patients activated the suicide alert and the research team intervened promptly with successful outcomes.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, 9% (3/34) of patients activated the suicide alert, and the research team promptly intervened with successful outcomes.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (primary care patients and health care workers) completing first self-assessment

evidence.title: Exploration of Mental Health and Stress Among Nursing Interns Through a Chatbot: A Single-Group Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Keyword-triggered chatbot alerts detecting high-risk distress expressions among nursing interns
evidence.effect: Chatbot flagged 16 high-risk expressions per 100 messages; suicidal ideation declined (10-4) pre/post, with no comparator and no evaluation of alert accuracy or response.
evidence.quote: The chatbot flagged 16 high-risk expressions per 100 messages, notably so tired and under pressure; 60.6% reported internship distress.

evidence.title: Solace, a Therapeutic Conversational Agent for Management of Chronic Pain: Acceptability and Usability Study
evidence.outcome: Whether chatbot safety guardrails handled suicidal ideation and injury risk in conversations
evidence.effect: Guardrails designed to identify and manage suicidal ideation and injury reported as performing appropriately during the study; no numbers given in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Safety guardrails designed to identify and manage instances of suicidal ideation, injury, or requests for medication recommendations performed appropriately during the study.

evidence.title: Suicide- and crisis-risk detection using large language models in mental-health chatbots
evidence.outcome: Real-time detection of suicide and crisis risk in chatbot conversation turns, including latency
evidence.effect: High and extreme-sensitivity variants achieved 98.9% and 100% recall with mean latency <1 s, showing real-time per-turn detection is feasible.
evidence.quote: High - and  extreme-sensitivity variants achieved near-perfect (98.9%) and perfect (100%) recall, demonstrating that near–zero–miss crisis detection from natural language is technically feasible in real time (mean latency <1 s).

evidence.title: An independent supervisory safety agent improves reaction of large language models to suicidal ideation
evidence.outcome: Detection of suicide risk requiring intervention, supervisory monitoring vs native LLM safeguards
evidence.effect: Supervisory system detected risk in 205/224 (91.5%) vs 41/224 (18.3%) for native safeguards; 166 of 168 discordant pairs favored supervisory system (matched OR ≈83.0).
evidence.quote: The supervisory system detected suicide risk in 205 of 224 evaluations (91.5%) versus 41 of 224 (18.3%) for native LLM safeguards.

evidence.title: Risk Governance for Generative AI Mental Health Support: A Multi-Turn Safety Architecture
evidence.outcome: Risk detection performance of real-time contextual risk detection in multi-turn mental health conversations
evidence.effect: Specificity 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity 0.92 (95%CI: 0.88;0.95); stable across conversation length and across two models.
evidence.quote: achieving high risk detection performance (specificity: 0.85 (95%CI: 0.78;0.91), sensitivity: 0.92 (95%CI: 0.88;0.95))

evidence.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Knowledge Graph and Large Language Model Hybrid Architecture for Multi-Modality Mental Health Counseling
evidence.outcome: Crisis detection sensitivity/specificity on adversarial probes and external dialogues
evidence.effect: Adversarial sensitivity 96.7%, specificity 95.4% (277 probes); detected 98.5% of 600 external dialogues with ongoing suicidal ideation or self-harm at or before the annotator confirming turn.
evidence.quote: Adversarial crisis-detection sensitivity was 96.7% and specificity 95.4% (277 probes); on external validation, the system detected 98.5% of 600 dialogues with ongoing suicidal ideation or self-harm at or before the annotator confirming turn.

evidence.title: Deterministic Retrieval-Grounded Language Models for Clinical Counseling: Large-Scale Multilingual Evaluation with Cryptographically Verifiable Pipelines
evidence.outcome: Effect of rule-based risk routing on safety scores in ablation
evidence.effect: Deterministic safety routing contributed significantly to performance, driving safety; safety scores 4.45/5 English and 4.77/5 Chinese; no system failures observed.
evidence.quote: Ablation experiments demonstrate that retrieval grounding and deterministic safety routing each contribute significantly to overall performance, with the former driving clinical fidelity and the latter driving safety.

evidence.title: An AI-based mental health guardrail and dataset for identifying psychiatric crises in text-based conversations
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of a guardrail detecting psychiatric crises in text messages
evidence.effect: On the Verily dataset, sensitivity 0.990, specificity 0.992, F1 0.939, category-level sensitivity 0.917-0.992, specificity ≥0.978. On the NVIDIA subset, sensitivity 0.982, accuracy 0.921, specificity 0.859.
evidence.quote: The VMHG demonstrated high sensitivity (0.990) and specificity (0.992) on the Verily dataset, with an F1-score of 0.939 and high category-level sensitivity (0.917-0.992) and specificity (≥0.978).

evidence.title: Automated Safety Testing and Reporting Application for Conversational Safety Monitoring of Generative AI Tools for Mental Health: Development and Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of automated external monitor detecting user self-harm/harm-to-others risk in chatbot conversations versus human consensus
evidence.effect: User self-harm detection was perfect (accuracy 1.00, sensitivity 1.00, kappa 1.00) including subtle cases; high-risk categories had errors in only 9/100 transcripts (7 false negatives).
evidence.quote: Notably, ASTRA had perfect agreement with expert human ratings on user indications of self-harm.

evidence.title: The efficacy, feasibility, and technical outcomes of a GPT-4o-based chatbot Amanda for relationship support: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Chatbot identification of potential safety concerns in interaction transcripts
evidence.effect: Amanda did not consistently identify potential safety concerns; authors call for enhanced risk detection capabilities before real-world deployment.
evidence.quote: However, limitations were noted: Amanda occasionally produced repetitive or generic responses and did not consistently identify potential safety concerns.

evidence.title: Delusions and Harms Associated with AI Chatbot Use: Early Evidence from 185 Real-World Reports
evidence.outcome: Chatbot validation of delusions and suicide outcomes in self-reported chatbot-associated mental health harms
evidence.effect: Delusional beliefs in 102 of 185 reports (55.1%); chatbot validation of beliefs in 50/102 (49.0%); four second-hand reports described death by suicide.
evidence.quote: Four second-hand reports described death by suicide.

evidence.title: Beyond Simulations: What 20,000 Real Conversations Reveal About Mental Health AI Safety
evidence.outcome: Suicide-risk cases lacking crisis resources and NSSI mentions lacking intervention
evidence.effect: Clinician review found zero suicide-risk cases without crisis resources. Three NSSI mentions (.015%) lacked intervention, implying a .38% lower-bound false negative rate.
evidence.quote: Three NSSI mentions (.015%) lacked intervention, implying a .38% lower-bound false negative rate.

evidence.title: Perinatal Engagement With a Purpose-Built AI for Mental Health (Ash): Emotional Expression, Help-Seeking, and Estimated Depression Trajectories Across Pregnancy and Postpartum
evidence.outcome: Missed or mishandled risk in mental health chatbot conversations, per clinician review
evidence.effect: Safety-relevant content in 11.0% of sessions; 0/50 confirmed safety gaps after clinician adjudication.
evidence.quote: Safety-relevant content appeared in 11.0% of sessions, with no confirmed safety gaps after clinician adjudication (0/50).

evidence.title: Substance-induced manic psychosis in which delusions were corroborated by a chatbot - case report
evidence.outcome: Chatbot response to a user with acute manic psychosis, including risk recognition
evidence.effect: In one patient, ChatGPT reportedly affirmed a 'spiritual awakening', minimised the possibility of mania, and discouraged antipsychotic medication. Causal contribution to the presentation could not be determined.
evidence.quote: This case demonstrates that, in patients with psychotic symptoms, AI chatbots may reinforce delusional beliefs and impair the development of insight, and may also interfere with engagement with treatment by providing advice that conflicts with clinical recommendations.

evidence.title: Assessing Risks of Large Language Models in Mental Health Support: A Framework for Automated Clinical AI Red Teaming
evidence.outcome: Chatbot handling of suicide risk in simulated therapy dialogue
evidence.effect: AI agents failed to de-escalate suicide risk across N=369 simulated sessions; no rate reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We identify specific iatrogenic risks, including the validation of patient delusions ("AI Psychosis") and failure to de-escalate suicide risk.

evidence.title: Lost in Delusion: Examining LLM Safety Under User Delusions and Distress
evidence.outcome: Failure to act on user distress in chatbot conversations with delusional framing
evidence.effect: Models fail to act on recognized distress when it is embedded in delusion, with safety interventions suppressed by up to 4.5x.
evidence.quote: This reveals a recognition-intervention gap: models detect distress at comparable rates regardless of framing, yet sharply fail to act on it once distress is embedded in delusion, with safety interventions suppressed by up to 4.5x.

evidence.title: Food Noise & False Safety: A Systematic Evaluation of How LLMs Fail to Adapt to Eating Disorder Queries with Clinician Feedback
evidence.outcome: Unsafe LLM responses to eating disorder prompts with varying risk levels
evidence.effect: Specific linguistic cues in prompts increased the likelihood of unsafe responses. LLMs uncritically adapted to problematic and potentially dangerous user inputs. No numeric results reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: We find, in consultation with clinical ED experts, that specific linguistic cues in prompts increase the likelihood of unsafe responses

evidence.title: Leveraging simulation to provide a practical framework for assessing the novel scope of risk of LLMs in healthcare
evidence.outcome: False-negative rates of LLMs detecting suicidal ideation, therapy requests, and therapy-like interactions in synthetic chatbot conversations
evidence.effect: Frequent errors in suicidal-ideation and therapy-like interactions; estimated P1 ranged 2.0×10-8 to 2.6×10-4 and P2 from 7.1×10-5 to 9.6×10-3, spanning up to four orders of magnitude across 14 models.
evidence.quote: LLM success at generating synthetic safety datasets varied substantially by task, with strong performance for neutral and non-therapeutic content but frequent errors in suicidal-ideation and therapy-like interactions.
evidence.sample_unit: open-source LLMs evaluated on synthetic safety-classification tasks

evidence.title: Companions Made of Code: Why Emotional AI Must Not Be Introduced into Mental Healthcare Without Regulation
evidence.outcome: Chatbot recognition of suicide-risk cues and guidance toward human help
evidence.effect: Exploratory test of eight widely available chatbots found systems frequently simulate empathy but fail to recognise suicide-risk cues or guide users toward human help. No numeric rates reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: It combines theoretical analysis with an exploratory examination of eight widely available chatbots, demonstrating that current systems frequently simulate empathy while failing to recognise suicide-risk cues or guide users toward human help.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Clinical Safety of LLMs in Response to High-Risk Mental Health Disclosures
evidence.outcome: Risk acknowledgment, help-seeking encouragement and resource provision in chatbot crisis responses
evidence.effect: Most models showed empathy, but few consistently provided practical support or kept the conversation open; none met clinical standards for crisis response.
evidence.quote: Notably, most models exhibited empathy, but few consistently provided practical support or kept the conversation open.

evidence.title: Prompt Engineering Limitations: Preliminary Evaluation of Large Language Models for Psychotherapy Safety
evidence.outcome: Chatbot handling of high-risk psychiatric scenarios, including self-harm endorsement, under therapy-principle prompting
evidence.effect: Prompt engineering reduced explicit endorsement of self-harm but consistently failed in ambiguous or clinically nuanced situations; models validated harmful statements, colluded with hallucinations, minimized symptoms.
evidence.quote: Prompt engineering reduced some predictable risks, such as explicit endorsement of self-harm, but consistently failed in ambiguous or clinically nuanced situations.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs tested on high-risk psychiatric scenarios

evidence.title: Conversational AI and Emerging Psychosis: A Simulation Study of Potentially Iatrogenic Response Patterns
evidence.outcome: Chatbot risk assessment and support in emerging psychosis conversations
evidence.effect: Problematic patterns across all systems, including omissions of assessment and support, premature recommendations, reinforcement of paranoid interpretations, and promotion of safety-seeking behaviours.
evidence.quote: Problematic patterns were observed across all systems, including omissions of assessment and support, premature recommendations, simulation of affective bonding, reinforcement of paranoid interpretations, and promotion of safety-seeking behaviours.

evidence.title: AI in Relationship Counselling: Evaluating ChatGPT’s Therapeutic Capabilities in Providing Relationship Advice
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT's assessment of risk during single-session relationship counselling
evidence.effect: Poor assessment of risk was identified as a limitation; no numeric results reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Limitations include a poor assessment of risk and reaching collaborative solutions with the participant.

evidence.title: Safety of Large Language Models in Addressing Depression
evidence.outcome: Chatbot recognition of and response to acute suicide risk, including crisis resources
evidence.effect: Few agents included crisis resources; only two referenced suicide hotlines; 22 of 25 agents resumed dialogue after risk reverted to a lower level despite insisting on human intervention.
evidence.quote: Despite the conversational agents insisting on human intervention, 22 out of 25 agents would eventually resume the dialogue if the simulation reverted to a lower risk level.

evidence.title: Describing the Framework for AI Tool Assessment in Mental Health and Applying It to a Generative AI Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder Platform: Tutorial
evidence.outcome: FAITA-Mental Health crisis management domain score for OCD Coach chatbot
evidence.effect: Framework identified gaps in acute crisis management for the generative AI OCD tool; no numeric scores reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: suggesting that the framework effectively identifies key strengths and gaps in AI-driven mental health tools, particularly in areas such as credibility, user experience, and acute crisis management.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Quality of Psychotherapy Conversational Agents: Framework Development and Cross-Sectional Study
evidence.outcome: Chatbot quality subscores for monitoring and risk evaluation section
evidence.effect: Monitoring and risk evaluation subscores were low at 0.67-0.75 across the 4 psychotherapy chatbots; authors conclude they failed to address essential safety functions adequately.
evidence.quote: Scores were low for the therapeutic orientation (subscores=0) and monitoring and risk evaluation sections (subscores=0.67-0.75).

evidence.title: Performance of mental health chatbot agents in detecting and managing suicidal ideation
evidence.outcome: Adequacy of chatbot responses to simulated escalating suicidal risk scenarios (C-SSRS-based prompts)
evidence.effect: None of 29 agents met the adequate-response criteria; 51.72% gave marginal responses and 48.28% were inadequate. Common errors: no emergency contact information and lack of contextual understanding.
evidence.quote: None of the tested agents satisfied our initial criteria for an adequate response, 51.72% satisfied the relaxed criteria for a marginal response, while 48.28% were deemed inadequate.

evidence.title: Generative AI for Eating Disorders: Linguistic Comparison With Online Support and Qualitative Analysis of Harms
evidence.venue: The International journal of eating disorders
evidence.outcome: Harmful content in AI chatbot responses to eating disorder peer-support posts, including missed emotional cues
evidence.effect: Clinician review of 100 AI responses found reinforcement of ED behaviors, implicit weight-loss bias, and insensitivity to emotional cues; all four chatbots produced harmful content to varying degrees.
evidence.quote: All AI chatbots produced responses containing harmful content, such as promoting ED behaviors or biases, to varying degrees.
evidence.sample_unit: Reddit posts (each with AI-generated responses; 100 AI responses qualitatively reviewed by clinicians)

evidence.title: ChatGPT Health performance in a structured test of triage recommendations
evidence.outcome: Activation of crisis-intervention messages across suicidal ideation presentations
evidence.effect: Crisis messages activated unpredictably, more often when patients described no specific method than when they did.
evidence.quote: Crisis-intervention messages activated unpredictably across suicidal ideation presentations, occurring more frequently when patients described no specific method than when they did.

evidence.title: Intelligent virtual agents in psychotherapy: a safety evaluation across high-risk mental health scenarios
evidence.outcome: Chatbot risk recognition and response to acute suicidality risk
evidence.effect: Key concerns included inadequate recognition of risk and insufficient referral to crisis resources; 29% problematic responses, 12.5% highly critical.
evidence.quote: Key concerns included inadequate recognition of risk, normalization of substance use, and insufficient referral to crisis resources, particularly in scenarios involving underage alcohol access and suicide-related inquiries.

evidence.title: Evaluating a Consumer LLM for Suicide Risk Response Calibration: A Pilot Study
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: Risk assessment and crisis response to suicide risk in consumer LLM outputs
evidence.effect: Model approximated clinical triage patterns, with escalation elements rising with risk, but showed critical limitations in detecting indirect suicidal expressions and was deemed unsuitable for autonomous crisis intervention.
evidence.quote: Overall, Gemini 2.5 Flash approximated clinical triage patterns but demonstrated critical limitations in detecting indirect suicidal expressions.

evidence.title: Between Help and Harm: An Evaluation of Mental Health Crisis Handling by LLMs
evidence.outcome: Appropriateness and safety of LLM responses to suicidal ideation and self-harm crisis inputs
evidence.effect: Many outputs, especially for self-harm and suicidal categories, were inappropriate or unsafe. gpt-4o-mini and grok-4-fast produced more unsafe responses; gpt-5-nano and deepseek-v3.2-exp had low harm rates.
evidence.quote: Many outputs, especially in self-harm and suicidal categories, are inappropriate or unsafe.

evidence.title: One Year Later...The Harms Persist, But So Do We!
evidence.outcome: LLM safeguard failure rates across 16 DSM-5 conditions under adversarial attack
evidence.effect: Safeguards held reliably only for suicide and self-harm; eating disorders, substance use disorder, and major depressive disorder showed failure rates of up to 100%.
evidence.quote: Results show that safeguards hold reliably only for suicide and self-harm, while conditions such as eating disorders, substance use disorder, and major depressive disorder exhibit failure rates of up to 100%.

evidence.title: Beyond the Flag: Clinical Framing Closes the Moderation Gap in Suicide Risk Measurement
evidence.outcome: Moderation API recovery of graded suicide risk severity versus high/low risk separation
evidence.effect: Moderation APIs reached 0.860 high-risk F1 but only 0.395 macro F1 for severity, and over-predicted the most severe category.
evidence.quote: Vendor moderation APIs separate low- from high-severity posts well (0.860 high-risk F1) but measure severity poorly (0.395 macro F1), systematically over-predicting the most severe category.

evidence.title: mpathic Psychologist-led AI Clinical Tests Suicide Benchmark (mPACT-S-v1.0)
evidence.outcome: LLM harmful versus clinically helpful responses in simulated suicide-risk conversations across four risk levels
evidence.effect: Models varied substantially on severity-weighted mPACT-S score; Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.2 scored highest, Grok 4.1 and Mistral Medium 3 lowest; harm avoidance exceeded active helpfulness.
evidence.quote: Models were generally more successful at avoiding harmful responses than at producing actively helpful ones, and the relationship between harm avoidance and clinically appropriate responding varied across systems.

evidence.title: Between Help and Harm: An Evaluation Study of Mental Health Crisis Handling by Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Appropriateness of LLM responses to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and violence crisis inputs (5-point Likert)
evidence.effect: Some models (gpt-5-nano, deepseek-v3.2-exp) had very low harmful response rates; others (gpt-4o-mini, Llama-4-Scout, grok-4-fast) had markedly higher unsafe output rates, especially in self-harm and suicidal ideation categories.
evidence.quote: A nonnegligible proportion of responses was rated as inappropriate or harmful, particularly in the self-harm and suicidal ideation categories.
evidence.sample_unit: user inputs (mental health crisis test examples)

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve studies test real-time risk detection and response in mental health chatbots, and most report high detection rates or lower harmful-content rates, but eight use simulated conversations, vignettes, or benchmarks and none randomized users. The evidence suggests such protocols can detect risk in test settings, while their effect on whether users in crisis reach timely human help remains largely unmeasured.

perspectives.view: Four real-deployment studies are observational. Three lack any comparator, and one compares a purpose-built system with general-purpose models rather than with the same system without safeguards. Offline studies that report sensitivity give values between 91.5% and 100%, and they agree with each other, but they measure detection rather than patient outcomes. Certainty is low after downgrading for risk of bias and indirectness.

In 20,000 real conversations, three self-harm mentions lacked intervention, implying a lower-bound false-negative rate of .38%. An external monitor produced 7 false negatives in high-risk categories across 100 synthetic transcripts. A supervisory layer detected 91.5% of risk vignettes versus 18.3% for native model safeguards, which suggests an added layer may catch errors the base model misses.

A per-turn detector ran with mean latency under 1 second, which suggests real-time screening is feasible. In one deployment, keyword alerts fired at 16 per 100 messages with no check of alert accuracy. Moderation tools separated high from low risk with F1 0.860 but graded severity with macro F1 0.395, so alert volume and triage fidelity may limit workflow fit.

Only one test included non-English use, an automated benchmark that scored safety at 4.77/5 in Chinese and 4.45/5 in English. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy participants, and most did not report the population. A hazard study found a model missed indirect suicidal expressions, and detection of such expressions in underserved groups remains untested.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot operators to implement protocols that respond in real time to acute risk of physical harm, so the practice is a legal duty in that state regardless of evidence strength. Eight of the twelve tests used simulated conversations or benchmarks, which leaves regulators limited real-world performance data for judging whether a protocol works.

Tested protocols pair automated detection with human responders. A research team handled 3 alerts among 34 users, and a multi-agent system with clinician oversight reported no safety-risk content among 12,040 real-user responses. No study reported staffing, response times at scale, or cost, and an alert rate of 16 per 100 messages suggests responder workload would grow with message volume.

Hazard studies show why the human handoff matters to users. In one, 22 of 25 agents resumed ordinary dialogue after risk appeared to fall, and in another none of 29 app agents gave an adequate response to escalating suicidal risk. Among tests of the practice, only one reports that people reached users who triggered alerts, with 3 of 34 users receiving prompt intervention.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized users or compared the same chatbot with and without a real-time risk protocol, and only one small study of 34 users reported what happened after an alert. Real-deployment studies with concurrent comparison are needed. They should report false-negative rates, time to human contact, responder workload, and outcomes such as crisis-service contact and self-harm events, and they should include delusional or indirect presentations where hazard studies show detection fails.
commentary.underserved_note: One automated benchmark tested Chinese-language counseling scenarios, and one deployment enrolled nursing interns in China. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations in the United States. Detection and response performance for these groups is therefore unknown, and health systems serving them would need local validation before relying on published accuracy figures.
